**** GENERAL PROVISIONS ****
§ 30.01 MAYOR AND TOWN COUNCIL.
   (A)   Town government structure. The town is classified as a town with a
population of fewer than 1,000. The town is governed by a Town Council
consisting of a Mayor and four Council members elected at large.
   (B)   Terms of office.
      (1)   All terms are four years.
      (2)   The Mayor and two Council members are elected in one cycle; the
other two Council members in the next.
      (3)   Terms begin at 12:00 p.m. on January 1 following the election.
      (4)   Vacancies are filled in accordance with the state code.
   (C)   Candidate eligibility.
      (1)   Must have been a resident of the town for at least 365 consecutive
days prior to the election;
      (2)   Must meet the qualifications in the state code;
      (3)   Residency in an annexed area for 365 days prior to the election
counts toward eligibility;
      (4)   Elected officials must maintain residency during their term;
      (5)   Establishing a principal residence outside of town results in
automatic vacancy (per state code);
      (6)   All candidates must be registered voters in the town; and
      (7)   Absence from town for over 60 consecutive days without Council
consent results in an automatic vacancy.
   (D)   Administrative authority. The Mayor holds executive authority and may
designate others to perform administrative duties as allowed by state law.
   (E)   Mayor’s duties. The Mayor shall:
      (1)   Enforce town laws and keep the peace;
      (2)   Execute laws, ordinances and resolutions;
      (3)   Report the condition of the town and recommend improvements;
      (4)   Make appointments with Council approval;
      (5)   Inspect town records;
      (6)   Oversee Town Council decorum;
      (7)   Ensure the Town Code is up to date;
      (8)   Appoint Planning Commission members with Council consent;
      (9)   Appoint Board members with Council consent; and
      (10)   Ensure a Hearing Officer is appointed.
   (F)   Town Council duties. The Town Council shall:
      (1)   Set policies and adopt ordinances to ensure public welfare;
      (2)   Serve as the legislative and policymaking body;
      (3)   Act as the appeal authority, applying existing law without
modification;
      (4)   Oversee financial policy and budgeting;
      (5)   Represent the interests of all citizens; and
      (6)   Refrain from exerting individual authority over town operations.
   (G)   Meeting minutes. Approved minutes constitute the official record and
shall be kept by the Town Recorder/Clerk and made available in accordance with
the state code.
   (H)   Code of conduct.
      (1)   Town Council members must preserve order and not interrupt
proceedings.
      (2)   All remarks must be respectful and limited to the matter at hand.
      (3)   Interruptions are only permitted for points of order.
      (4)   Debate must remain issue focused and avoid personal attacks.
   (I)   Compensation. The compensation to be paid to each elected and
appointed office of the town shall be established by the Town Council by
ordinance.
   (J)   Modifying the Mayor’s duties. The Council may reassign administrative
duties by ordinance (per state code). Legislative, judicial, ceremonial and ex
officio powers of the Mayor may not be reassigned.
   (K)   Land use authority. See §§
154.030 through
154.048.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.110) (Ord. 2024-06, passed 5-9-2024)
**** MEETINGS ****
§ 30.15 REGULAR MEETINGS.
   The governing body shall hold one regular meeting per month unless otherwise
deemed necessary by the Town Council.
(Prior Code, § 1.3.10)
§ 30.16 DEFINITIONS.
   For the purpose of this subchapter, the following definitions shall apply
unless the context clearly indicates or requires a different meaning.
   ANCHOR LOCATION. The physical location where the public may attend an
electronic meeting.
   CATASTROPHIC EVENT. A major event such as an earthquake or pandemic that
prevents in-person meetings.
   CHAIR. The presiding officer of the public meeting, responsible for
maintaining order and ensuring adherence to the code of conduct.
   DEPUTY SHERIFF OR DESIGNEE. The law enforcement officer or appointed
individual responsible for enforcing the rules of the public meeting, including
the removal of individuals who violate the code of conduct.
   ELECTRONIC MEETING. A meeting where one or more members participate via
telephonic or video conferencing technology.
   EMERGENCY MEETING. A meeting called under urgent circumstances where normal
notice requirements may be impractical.
   OPEN AND PUBLIC MEETINGS ACT (OPMA). A set of state laws ensuring
transparency in government meetings.
   PUBLIC BODY. An administrative, advisory, executive or legislative body of
the state or its political subdivisions that:
      (1)   Is created by the Utah Constitution, statute, rule, ordinance or
resolution;
      (2)   Consists of two or more persons;
      (3)   Expends, disburses or is supported in whole or in part by tax
revenue; and
      (4)   It is vested with the authority to make decisions regarding the
public’s business.
   PUBLIC COMMENT. A portion of the public meeting designated for individuals
to address the public body on agenda items or other matters within its
jurisdiction.
   PUBLIC MEETING. A gathering of a quorum of the Town Council or any
commission or board where public business is discussed or decided.
   PUBLIC NOTICE. The process of informing the public about the date, time,
place and agenda of a public meeting, as required by state law.
   QUORUM. The minimum number of members required to be present for the public
body to conduct its business legally.
   ROLL CALL VOTE. A voting method where each member states his or her vote
individually for recordkeeping purposes.
   SUBSTANTIAL RISK DETERMINATION. A written finding by the Chair of a public
body that the anchor location of a meeting presents a substantial health or
safety risk, allowing a meeting to be conducted entirely electronically under
state code.
(Prior Code, § 1.3.20)
§ 30.17 EMERGENCY MEETINGS.
   Emergency meetings may be called only when immediate action is required, and
normal noticing would be detrimental to the town. The following requirements
apply.
   (A)   The Mayor or any two Town Council members may order an emergency
meeting.
   (B)   The order shall be recorded in the Town Council minutes.
   (C)   The meeting must comply with the Open Public Meetings Act, being
U.C.A. Title 52, Chapter 4, regarding notice.
   (D)   Notice shall be provided to each Council member who did not sign the
order via personal delivery, delivery to his or her residence or electronic
means (text or e-mail).
   (E)   A Council member’s attendance at the emergency meeting waives the
notice requirement.
   (F)   The written notice must specify the meeting’s time, place and purpose.
(Prior Code, § 1.3.30)
§ 30.18 OPEN MEETINGS.
   All meetings shall be open to the public unless closed pursuant to the state
code.
(Prior Code, § 1.3.40)
§ 30.19 CLOSED MEETINGS.
   (A)   Authority to close. A closed meeting may be held only in accordance
with the State Open and Public Meetings Act, U.C.A. §§ 52-4-204 through 52-4-
206.
   (B)   Procedure. A public body may vote to close a meeting following the
requirements and procedures set forth in U.C.A. § 52-4-204.
   (C)   Permitted purposes. Closed meetings may be held only for the purposes
outlined in U.C.A. § 52-4-205.
   (D)   Records. The recording, minutes and sworn statement requirements for
closed meetings shall comply with U.C.A. § 52-4-206.
   (E)   Prohibited actions. No ordinance, resolution, rule, regulation,
contract or appointment may be approved in a closed meeting.
(Prior Code, § 1.3.45)
§ 30.20 ELECTRONIC MEETINGS.
   (A)   Authority and purpose. Pursuant to state code, the town establishes
procedures for electronic meetings to allow full participation by members of
public bodies, regardless of their physical location.
   (B)   Participation in electronic meetings.
      (1)   Public bodies may convene electronic meetings as necessary.
      (2)   Unless otherwise noted in the agenda, public body members may
participate electronically.
      (3)   Public body members must notify the meeting administrator in
advance to ensure electronic access.
   (C)   Quorum requirement. A quorum must be present either in person or
electronically for an electronic meeting to proceed.
   (D)   Meeting administration.
      (1)   The meeting administrator shall announce the participants and
ensure that public attendees at the anchor location can hear the proceedings.
      (2)   No more than three members may participate electronically at one
time.
      (3)   At least two members must be physically present at the anchor
location unless a written determination by the Chair states that an anchor
location poses a substantial health or safety risk, per state code.
   (E)   Technical disruptions. If a participating member is disconnected, the
presiding officer shall determine whether to continue the meeting, attempt to
reconnect or adjust the agenda accordingly, provided a quorum remains.
   (F)   Recordkeeping. Electronic meetings shall be conducted, recorded and
documented in compliance with all open meeting and recordkeeping laws.
   (G)   Catastrophic events. In the event of a catastrophic event (e.g.,
earthquake, pandemic), electronic meetings may be held as mandated by state
law.
(Prior Code, § 1.3.50)
§ 30.21 QUORUM.
   (A)   A quorum consists of three or more Town Council members.
   (B)   No official action may be taken without a quorum. A meeting with fewer
than a quorum may adjourn but may not conduct business.
(Prior Code, § 1.3.60)
§ 30.22 VOTING.
   (A)   Roll call votes.
      (1)   A roll call vote with “yes” or “no” is required for all ordinances,
resolutions and any action creating a liability for the town.
      (2)   A roll call vote shall be taken upon request by any Council member.
      (3)   Ordinances and resolutions must be in writing before a vote is
taken.
   (B)   Minimum votes required.
      (1)   A majority of the quorum is required to pass any action, but never
fewer than three votes, regardless of absences or vacancies (see state code).
      (2)   Any action failing to meet the required votes is considered
defeated.
   (C)   Filling Council vacancies.
      (1)   If a Council vacancy exists, a majority of the remaining members
may vote to fill the vacancy pursuant to state code.
      (2)   If more than three seats are vacant, the remaining members shall
appoint replacements until a quorum is restored.
   (D)   Reconsideration of actions. No action may be reconsidered or rescinded
at a special meeting unless the number of attending Council members is equal to
or greater than the number present when the action was initially approved.
(Prior Code, § 1.3.70)
§ 30.23 ORDER OF BUSINESS.
   (A)   (1)   The Town Recorder/Clerk shall maintain a written record of all
Council meetings.
      (2)   Minutes of closed meetings shall remain confidential unless made
public by Council action or court order.
   (B)   The Town Council shall conduct town business according to the posted
agenda. However, the Council may, by motion, amend the agenda during the
meeting, including reordering, adding or removing items as needed.
   (C)   The Recorder/Clerk is responsible for preparing, drafting and posting
the agenda, including the items and their order as provided by the Mayor.
   (D)   Any Council member may propose an item for the agenda with the
approval of the Mayor or an additional Council member.
(Prior Code, § 1.3.80)
§ 30.24 PUBLIC COMMENT PROCEDURE.
   (A)   The Town Council may establish rules governing public comment to
ensure order and efficiency.
   (B)   Speakers shall state their name for the record and limit remarks to
the time allotted by the presiding officer.
   (C)   The presiding officer may terminate comments that are profane,
irrelevant or repetitive.
   (D)   The presiding officer may have disruptive persons removed from a
meeting.
(Prior Code, § 1.3.90)
§ 30.25 ACCESSIBILITY AND ADA COMPLIANCE.
   (A)   All public meetings shall comply with the Americans with Disabilities
Act (ADA), being 42 U.S.C. §§ 12101 et seq.
   (B)   Reasonable accommodations will be made upon request to the Town
Recorder/Clerk at least 48 hours before the meeting.
   (C)   Meeting agendas and materials shall be made available in accessible
formats where feasible.
(Prior Code, § 1.3.100)
§ 30.26 CODE OF CONDUCT FOR CITIZENS AND VISITORS.
   (A)   General behavior. Attendees must maintain decorum, avoiding personal
attacks, profanity or disruptive behavior. The Chair may direct the removal of
individuals violating these standards, who may also face penalties under this
code or the state code.
   (B)   Audience participation. Unauthorized remarks or disruptive
demonstrations are prohibited, such as stomping of feet, whistles, yelling and
similar demonstrations. The Chair may direct the removal of offenders and
initiate prosecution if necessary.
   (C)   Prohibited items. Placards, banners or signs are not allowed in
meeting rooms. Exhibits and visual aids for presentations are permitted but
must be reviewed by staff prior to the meeting.
   (D)   Law enforcement role. The town-appointed law enforcement officer,
serving as the chief law enforcement officer, shall be present at Council
meetings when necessary unless excused by the Mayor. This officer shall act as
sergeant-at-arms for the Town Council and provide assistance as needed to
enforce the rules of the Council.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.190) Penalty, see §
10.99
   ORDINANCES, CODES AND RESOLUTIONS
§ 30.40 GENERAL REQUIREMENTS AS TO FORM.
   (A)   All ordinances and codified laws shall be signed by the Mayor (or
Mayor Pro Tempore in the Mayor’s absence), each voting Council member and
attested by the Town Recorder/Clerk. An ordinance is not enforceable without
the required signatures.
   (B)   Ordinances become effective upon final passage unless a later
effective date is specified within the ordinance.
   (C)   If no effective date is specified, the ordinance shall take effect on
the earlier of: 20 days after publication/posting; or 30 days after final
passage by the Town Council.
(Prior Code, § 1.7.10)
§ 30.41 DEFINITIONS.
   For the purpose of this subchapter, the following definitions shall apply
unless the context clearly indicates or requires a different meaning.
   CODE. A systematically arranged and codified collection of the town’s
general ordinances, organized by subject matter and assigned a unique title,
chapter and section number.
   CODIFICATION. The process of arranging, organizing, numbering and
incorporating adopted ordinances into the official Town Code Book.
   DOCUMENT CONTROL CHANGES. A notation placed at the end of a code section or
ordinance indicating the ordinance number and date of adoption or revision
(e.g., Ord. 2025-01 passed 1-19-2025). Used to track legislative history.
   EFFECTIVE DATE. The date on which an ordinance or resolution becomes legally
enforceable. This may be upon passage, after publication/posting, or on a
specific date as set forth in the document.
   ORDINANCE. A legislative act adopted by the Town Council with the force of
law. ORDINANCES are required for creating regulations, imposing penalties or
levying taxes.
   RESERVED SECTION. A placeholder section is marked as (Reserved) to preserve
numbering space for future use without renumbering existing sections.
   RESOLUTION. A formal expression of opinion, policy or intent by the Town
Council. RESOLUTIONS are used for administrative actions and do not carry the
force of law unless specifically authorized by statute.
   TITLE. The highest level in the code organization, representing broad areas
of municipal regulation (e.g., Administration, Land Use, Public Safety).
   VACANT TITLE/CHAPTER/SECTION. Unused numbers are intentionally left blank to
allow for future expansion without disrupting the numerical structure of the
code.
(Prior Code, § 1.7.20)
§ 30.42 ORDINANCE FORMAT.
   Each ordinance adopted by the Town Council shall include the following
elements in substantially this order.
   (A)   Title, section, name and ordinance number.
      (1)   Title. Identifies the subject area (e.g., Title 15: Land Use);
      (2)   Section. Specifies the location within the title;
      (3)   Name. Describes the purpose (e.g., Soil Ordinance); and
      (4)   Ordinance number. Based on the adoption date in the format YYYY-XX,
with YYYY being the four-digit year and XX being a sequential number assigned
in order of adoption for that calendar year.
   (B)   Document control changes. A line showing the history of the ordinance,
including the date of creation, amendments and dates of revision;
   (C)   Ordinance body. The full text and provisions of the ordinance;
   (D)   Penalty clause (if applicable). A statement outlining the penalty for
violations or a reference to another ordinance that defines penalties or
classifications;
   (E)   Effective date. A statement identifying when the ordinance becomes
effective, either upon passage or after publication/posting; and
   (F)   Signatures.
      (1)   Line for Mayor or Mayor Pro Tempore;
      (2)   Lines for each Council member with a voting record; and
      (3)   Line for the Town Recorder/Clerk’s attestation and Town Seal.
(Prior Code, § 1.7.30)
§ 30.43 CODE FORMAT.
   Codified ordinances shall follow the town’s period-separated numbering
format, identifying:
      (A)   Title. The general category (e.g., Title 15: Land Use);
      (B)   Chapter. The specific subject (e.g., Chapter 150 – Building
Requirements);
      (C)   Section. The individual provision (e.g., § 150.01). Example: §
150.01, where 15 is the title number, 150 is the chapter number and 150.01 is
the section number.
      (D)   Document history. Line showing revisions and adoption references
(e.g., (Prior Code, § 10.1.10) (Ord. 2010-01, passed 1-1-2010)); and
      (E)   Vacant sections.
         (1)   Titles use odd numbers to allow expansion;
         (2)   Sections are numbered sequentially; and
         (3)   Reserved titles are labeled (Reserved) to preserve numbering
consistency and allow future growth.
(Prior Code, § 1.7.40)
§ 30.44 RESOLUTION FORMAT.
   (A)   Purpose and limitations. The Town Council may adopt resolutions to
manage administrative matters, including, but not limited to:
      (1)   Establishing water or utility rates;
      (2)   Setting garbage collection charges and service fees;
      (3)   Approving personnel policies and procedures; and
      (4)   Regulating use of town property.
   (B)   Restrictions. Resolutions shall not be used to impose criminal
penalties, fines or forfeitures. Those actions must be taken by ordinance.
   (C)   Form and numbering. Resolutions shall be formatted similarly to
ordinances, including a clear title, structured sections and a summary of the
adopted action.
      (1)   Each resolution shall be assigned a number using the following
format: RYYYY-XX.
      (2)   R stands for Resolution.
      (3)   YYYY is the four-digit year in which the resolution is adopted.
      (4)   XX is a sequential number assigned in order of adoption for that
calendar year.
      (5)   Example: R2025-03 would indicate the third resolution passed in the
year 2025.
   (D)   Effective date and publication.
      (1)   Resolutions do not require publication to become effective.
      (2)   A resolution may take effect immediately upon passage or on a later
date as specified by the Town Council.
      (3)   No resolution may become effective more than three months after its
date of passage.
      (4)   For public transparency, resolutions will be available in the
following places:
         (a)   At the Town Office;
         (b)   The town’s website; and
         (c)   The state’s public notice website.
(Prior Code, § 1.7.50)
§ 30.45 EMERGENCY ORDINANCES.
   In accordance with U.C.A. § 10-3-714, the Town Council may pass an emergency
ordinance effective immediately upon adoption, if necessary for the immediate
preservation of public peace, health or safety. The ordinance shall state the
reasons for the emergency and require a two-thirds vote of the Council.
(Prior Code, § 1.7.60)

§ 31.01 OATH OF OFFICE.
   Each elected or appointed officer shall take the oath of office prescribed
by U.C.A. § 52-1-8 before assuming duties. The oath shall be filed with the
Town Recorder/Clerk.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.260)
§ 31.02 OFFICIAL SEAL.
   The town shall maintain an official seal bearing the name “Fairfield, Utah.”
The Town Recorder/Clerk shall have custody of the seal and shall affix it to
official documents as required by law.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.270)
§ 31.03 ETHICS TRAINING REQUIREMENT.
   All elected and appointed officials shall complete annual ethics training as
required under the State Municipal Officers and Employees Ethics Act, being
U.C.A. Title 10, Chapter 3, Part 13. The Town Recorder/Clerk shall maintain
records of completion.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.280)
§ 31.04 TERM LIMITS AND VACANCIES.
   (A)   No elected official shall serve more than two consecutive full terms
in the same office.
   (B)   Vacancies in elected or appointed offices shall be filled in
accordance with U.C.A. § 20A-1-510 and Town Council policy.
   (C)   Service for less than one-half of a term shall not count toward the
term-limit calculation.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.290)
§ 31.05 APPOINTMENT; CODE OF CONDUCT; BOND REQUIREMENTS; COMPENSATION.
   (A)   Code of conduct. All staff must follow the same conduct standards as
Council members. The Mayor is responsible for enforcing staff decorum during
meetings.
   (B)   Bond requirements. 
      (1)   Officials must be bonded as required by the state code or town
ordinance. The State Money Management Council directives may supersede
Treasurer bond rules.
      (2)   The town pays for bonding premiums, and blanket bonds, covering
multiple officials under one policy, are permitted.
   (C)   Compensation. The compensation schedule attached to the ordinance
codified in this section as Exhibit A is approved and adopted to hereafter set
the compensation of those elected and appointed officials and town employees
referenced therein. Changes to said schedule shall be by ordinance.
   (D)   Other officers. The Council may appoint additional officers as needed,
define duties and set terms and compensation.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.130) (Ord. 2024-07, passed 6-26-2024; Ord. 2024-08, passed
6-26-2024)
§ 31.06 TOWN RECORDER/CLERK AND DEPUTY.
   The Town Recorder/Clerk and Deputy are appointed by the Mayor with Council
approval. The Recorder/Clerk shall perform all duties required by law and by
ordinance. The position of Recorder/Clerk shall be a full-time position,
allowing for certain benefits and compensation commensurate to the position as
outlined in the town’s policies and procedures, pursuant to a contract between
the town and the Recorder/Clerk.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.130) (Ord. 2024-07, passed 6-26-2024)
§ 31.07 TREASURER.
   (A)   The Town Treasurer is appointed by the Mayor with Council approval.
   (B)   The Treasurer shall:
      (1)   Manage all town funds, including budgeting and expenditures, and
maintain accurate financial records.
      (2)   Issue receipts and perform additional duties as required by
ordinance or law.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.130)
§ 31.08 TOWN ATTORNEY.
   (A)   Appointment. The Town Council shall appoint a Town Attorney, who shall
serve at the pleasure of the Council.
   (B)   Qualifications. The Town Attorney shall be duly licensed to practice
law in the state and in good standing with the Utah State Bar.
   (C)   Duties. The Town Attorney shall:
      (1)   Serve as legal advisor to the Mayor, Town Council and town staff;
      (2)   Prepare or review all contracts, ordinances, resolutions and other
legal documents involving the town;
      (3)   Represent the town in civil or administrative proceedings as
directed by the Town Council; and
      (4)   Perform such other duties as may be assigned by the Town Council or
required by law.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.140)
§ 31.09 ADMINISTRATIVE LAW JUDGE (HEARING OFFICER).
   (A)   Appointment. The Mayor shall appoint one or more Administrative Law
Judges, also known as Hearing Officers, to conduct hearings and render
decisions on matters authorized by town ordinance or state law as needed.
   (B)   Qualifications. The Administrative Law Judge shall possess
qualifications appropriate to the matters under their jurisdiction and may, but
need not, be a licensed attorney.
   (C)   Duties and authority. The Administrative Law Judge shall:
      (1)   Conduct quasi-judicial hearings as assigned by the Mayor or Town
Council or ordinance, including, but not limited to, appeals, enforcement
proceedings and determinations of administrative penalties;
      (2)   Administer oaths, receive testimony and evidence and issue written
findings and decisions;
      (3)   Ensure hearings are conducted in accordance with due process and
applicable town and state procedures; and
      (4)   Submit decisions or recommendations to the Mayor, Town Council,
Planning Commission or appeal authority, as appropriate.
   (D)   Independence. The Administrative Law Judge shall act impartially and
independently in all assigned matters and shall not be subject to the direction
or control of any town officer regarding the substance of decisions.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.150)
§ 31.10 CHIEF OF POLICE.
   The County Sheriff shall be the chief law enforcement officer of the town.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.170)
§ 31.11 FIRE CHIEF.
   (A)   Designation of Fire Chief. The Town Council shall designate a Fire
Chief or contracting fire authority to serve as the chief fire official for the
town.
   (B)   Authority and duties. The Fire Chief, or contracted fire authority,
shall:
      (1)   Be responsible for the administration, management and coordination
of all fire protection, prevention and emergency response services within the
town;
      (2)   Enforce applicable provisions of this code, the State Fire Code and
related state laws; and
      (3)   Perform all duties and responsibilities assigned by the Town
Council, interlocal agreement or applicable contract.
   (C)   Current provider. Until otherwise designated by ordinance or
interlocal agreement, the County Fire Marshal shall serve as the Town Fire
Chief.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.180)
§ 31.12 CHIEF ADMINISTRATIVE OFFICER.
   (A)   Designation of Chief Administrative Officer (CAO). The CAO shall
establish, manage and maintain an ongoing privacy and records management
program consistent with state law and the privacy program framework.
   (B)   Appointment of Records Officer(s). The CAO shall appoint Records
Officer(s). Records Officer(s) will implement and maintain privacy and records
practices as detailed in the agency’s privacy program and framework guidance.
   (C)   Roles and responsibilities.
      (1)   CAO responsibilities. Develop and maintain formal privacy and
records policies and procedures. Oversee their effective implementation
throughout the agency. Report the CAO designation to the Division of Archives
and Records Service (OARS), consistent with statute.
      (2)   Records officer responsibilities. Manage care, maintenance,
scheduling, classification, retention, disposal, access and preservation of
records. Execute all records and privacy policies established by the CAO.
(Res. 2025-18, passed 10-15-2025)

**** GENERAL ADMINISTRATIVE POLICIES ****
§ 32.001 NEPOTISM.
   (A)   Prohibited. No elected or appointed officer or town employee shall
employ, appoint or vote to appoint a relative to any position or employment
where the salary, wages or compensation is paid from public funds.
   (B)   Definitions. For the purpose of this section, the following
definitions shall apply unless the context clearly indicates or requires a
different meaning.
      APPOINTED OFFICER. An individual who has been appointed to a public
office or position within the town by an elected official or governing body.
      APPOINTMENT. The act of selecting or assigning a person to a position or
office, whether through election, appointment or other means, within the town’s
governance.
      DIRECT HIRING AUTHORITY. The power to hire, appoint or employ an
individual to a position within the town, typically vested in an elected
official, appointed officer or governing body.
      ELECTED OFFICER. An individual who has been elected to a public office
within the town, including, but not limited to, the Mayor or Town Council
members.
      EMPLOYEE. Any person employed by the town, regardless of position, who
receives compensation from public funds.
      PUBLIC FUNDS. Financial resources that are derived from taxpayer
contributions and allocated for use by the town for its operations, including
salaries, wages and compensation for employees.
      RELATIVE. Includes individuals related by blood or marriage
(consanguinity or affinity), such as: father, mother, spouse, son, daughter,
sister, brother, uncle, aunt, nephew, niece, first cousin, mother-in-law,
father-in-law, brother-in-law, sister-in-law, son-in-law or daughter-in-law.
      UNANIMOUS APPROVAL. A situation where every member of the Town Council or
relevant decision-making body agrees or votes in favor of a specific action,
such as the hiring or appointment of an employee or officer.
   (C)   Exceptions. This section does not apply to the following situations:
      (1)   If the employee was already employed by the town before the
relative assumed their public position;
      (2)   If the employee qualifies for the position based on compliance with
civil service or merit system laws, or certification by an authorized state or
municipal agency;
      (3)   The appointee will be employed for a period of 12 weeks or less;
      (4)   If the employee is the only available, qualified or eligible
candidate for the position; and/or
      (5)   If the employee’s appointment is approved by the Town Council.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.160) Penalty, see §
10.99
§ 32.002 CONFLICT OF INTEREST.
   (A)   Purpose. The purpose of this section is to ensure that all public
officers and employees of the town conduct the business of the town with
integrity, impartiality and transparency, in compliance with the State Public
Officers’ and Employees’ Ethics Act (U.C.A. Title 67, Chapter 16) and the
Municipal Officers’ and Employees’ Ethics Act (U.C.A. Title 10, Chapter 3, Part
13).
   (B)   Disclosure of conflicts. Every public official serving on the Town
Council, Planning Commission or any other officially appointed body of the town
must disclose any conflict of interest prior to participating in discussions or
decisions on the matter. A conflict of interest exists if the official, or a
close family member (including a spouse, parent, sibling, child or household
member), an employer, employee, agent, client or business associate:
      (1)   Is required to disclose a conflict under the State Municipal
Officers’ and Employees’ Ethics Act;
      (2)   Has an ownership interest in a business with matters under
consideration by the public body;
      (3)   Owns property within the town that is subject to zoning,
conditional use or development approvals;
      (4)   Acts as an agent, consultant or representative for an entity with
business before the public body;
      (5)   Has an ownership interest in a business that operates, is licensed
or provides services within the town, and which:
         (a)   Offers the same goods, services or development uses as another
business with matters under consideration; or
         (b)   Would be directly impacted financially by decisions under
consideration by the public body.
      (6)   Has an agreement with a party seeking approval that would provide
direct financial benefit if approval is granted.
   (C)   Conduct at public meetings. Officials with a conflict of interest must
disclose the conflict before the matter is discussed. Such officials shall not
participate in discussions, vote on the matter or chair that portion of the
meeting. However, they may provide input as private citizens. Exceptions may be
made if a majority of the remaining members determine that their input is
necessary for proper consideration of the matter.
   (D)   Participation in other public body meetings. A public official with a
conflict of interest may attend meetings of other public bodies where the
matter is being considered, but must disclose the conflict before speaking.
   (E)   Abstention from voting. Any public official required to disclose a
conflict must abstain from voting on the matter. If the official insists on
voting, his or her vote shall be recorded as an abstention and will not be
counted toward the total vote tally.
   (F)   Suspension of rules. These conflict of interest provisions may not be
suspended by vote or action of the Town Council or Planning Commission. Ethical
standards established by state law are mandatory and not subject to waiver or
modification.
   (G)   Violations and penalties. Failure to disclose a known conflict of
interest is a violation under the state code. It may result in removal from
office or other disciplinary action in accordance with the state code.
   (H)   Training and acknowledgment.
      (1)   All elected and appointed officials shall complete ethics training
as required by U.C.A. § 10-3-1315 at least once during each elected or
appointed term of office.
      (2)   All members of public bodies, including the Town Council, Planning
Commission and any advisory boards, shall complete Open and Public Meetings Act
training annually, as required by U.C.A. § 52-4-104.
      (3)   The Town Recorder/Clerk shall maintain records of all training
completion certificates and acknowledgments of receipt of these conflict of
interest provisions.
      (4)   Each official shall sign an acknowledgment of receipt and
understanding of these provisions and shall submit proof of training completion
to the Town Recorder/Clerk.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.200)
§ 32.003 RECORDS ACCESS AND MANAGEMENT.
   (A)   Adoption of state standards. The town adopts all relevant provisions
of the Government Records Access and Managements Act (GRAMA), being U.C.A.
Title 63G, Chapter 2, Part 1, as amended. Town records shall be classified and
managed in accordance with GRAMA standards.
   (B)   Fees. The town shall establish reasonable fees for duplicating
requested records, as set forth in the Town Fee Schedule.
   (C)   Retention. Town records shall be retained in accordance with GRAMA,
being U.C.A. Title 63G, Chapter 2, Part 1, as amended, and the state code. The
town reserves the right to maintain records beyond the retention periods
specified in the state retention schedule except for text messages which have a
retention period of seven days.
   (D)   Appeals. Appeals regarding access to government records shall follow
the procedures and timelines established in GRAMA, being U.C.A. Title 63G,
Chapter 2, Part 1, as amended. The Town Council shall serve as the designated
appeals board.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.210)
§ 32.004 FRAUD AND ABUSE REPORTING.
   (A)   Submission of complaints. Complaints related to fraud and abuse should
be submitted in writing. Complainants are encouraged to provide any evidence
that supports their claims at the time of submission.
   (B)   Essential information. The following essential information should be
included:
      (1)   Specific details regarding the incident (who, what, where, when).
      (2)   Any additional information that may assist in the investigation,
such as witness statements, documents or other pertinent evidence; and
      (3)   Due to limited resources, the town is unable to process complaints
that are vague or lack credible supporting evidence. Complaints should be
submitted using the following methods:
         (a)   E-mail: (Info@fairfieldtown-ut.gov); or
         (b)   U.S. Mail: Fairfield, PO Box 271, Cedar Valley, Utah 84013.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.220)
§ 32.005 TRAVEL BY EMPLOYEES; REIMBURSEMENT.
   (A)   Travel authorization. Employees must obtain advance authorization for
all travel through their supervisory system. Employees are responsible for
understanding travel procedures and providing documentation of travel-related
expenses and activities before traveling.
   (B)   Approval requirements.
      (1)   In-state travel must be approved in advance by the department
manager.
      (2)   Out-of-state travel requires advance approval from the Mayor.
      (3)   Proof of prior approval must be attached to the travel expense
reimbursement form.
   (C)   Expense reimbursement.
      (1)   Employees traveling together must submit separate reimbursement
vouchers; ensuring no duplicate claims.
      (2)   Employees must sign all vouchers before submission.
      (3)   All expenses must be strictly business-related.
   (D)   Receipt requirements.
      (1)   Original or copies of itemized receipts must be attached to the
reimbursement vouchers.
      (2)   Receipts must be dated and include the names of all individuals
covered by the expense to prevent duplicate reimbursements.
   (E)   Approval and submission.
      (1)   The reimbursement voucher must be signed by both the department
manager and the Mayor.
      (2)   Employees must clearly state the purpose of travel on the voucher.
      (3)   Travel costs for business associates, vendors or family members
accompanying an employee are not eligible for reimbursement.
      (4)   Reimbursement requests must be submitted within 30 days of the
travel or event.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.210)
§ 32.006 PERSONAL USE OF ENTITY ASSETS BY EMPLOYEES.
   (A)   Use restrictions. Employees may not use town resources for personal
gain unless:
      (1)   Use is available to the public on equal terms;
      (2)   Use is minimal and incidental; or
      (3)   Use is allowed by specific policy or ordinance.
   (B)   Incidental use criteria. Permitted only if:
      (1)   It complies with all policies;
      (2)   It does not interfere with town operations;
      (3)   It does not involve solicitation or for-profit activities;
      (4)   It does not involve illegal activity; or
      (5)   It does not damage public trust.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.240)
§ 32.007 SECURITY OF FILE CABINETS, COMPUTERS.
   (A)   File cabinets. Must be locked when not supervised. Access is
restricted to the Mayor, Recorder/Clerk, Deputy Recorder/Clerk and Financial
Officer.
   (B)   Computer security.
      (1)   All data is considered town property unless stated otherwise.
      (2)   The Mayor or designee oversees information security.
      (3)   Access to data is on a “need-to-know” basis.
      (4)   Users must report security issues to the Mayor or Council.
   (C)   Passwords.
      (1)   Minimum eight characters with uppercase and number/special
characters;
      (2)   Expires every 365 days;
      (3)   Cannot reuse the last three passwords;
      (4)   May not be stored or shared; and
      (5)   Must be changed if compromised or if the user changes.
   (D)   Portable devices. Confidential data must be encrypted. Lost or stolen
devices must be reported and passwords changed immediately.
   (E)   Policy violations. Violations may lead to disciplinary action,
including termination or legal action.
(Prior Code, § 1.1.250)

**** ANNEXATION POLICY ****
§ 32.020 PURPOSE.
   (A)   (1)   The intent of this subchapter is to guide decisions regarding
future annexations and ensure alignment with objectives in the town’s general
plan or future general plan.
      (2)   It will identify potential annexation areas and establish specific
standards and criteria that will guide the town’s decision on whether to grant
future annexation petitions in those areas.
      (3)   It would also help the town to prepare for any financial and
operational impacts of annexation while striving to protect the public health,
safety and welfare of the town’s existing and future residents.
   (B)   This subchapter was prepared in accordance with the requirements of
U.C.A. § 10-2-401.5, which requires all municipalities to adopt an annexation
policy plan before annexing an unincorporated area into the town.
(Res. R2024-17, passed 8-14-2024)
§ 32.021 EXPANSION AREA MAP.
   The Town Annexation Area Map, attached to the resolution codified in this
section as Exhibit 1, illustrates the town’s proposed future expansion areas.
This map represents the town’s growth boundaries and includes areas outside,
but adjacent to, its incorporated borders, which may be annexed into the town.
Proposed annexation areas must fall within the approved annexation declaration
area for town consideration. However, although property or properties may be
within a designated expansion area, compliance with this plan does not
guarantee approval.
(Res. R2024-17, passed 8-14-2024)
§ 32.022 ANNEXATION CRITERIA.
   The following list will guide the town’s decision on whether to grant future
annexation requests. All future requests for annexation will be evaluated
against the following criteria required by U.C.A. § 10-2-402.
   (A)   Any annexed area must be a contiguous area.
   (B)   The town will attempt to avoid gaps between or overlaps with expansion
areas of other municipalities.
   (C)   If the annexation is by petition, the proposed annexation area cannot
create an unincorporated island or peninsula unless the town and the county
agree to such creation.
   (D)   Annexation requests cannot propose the annexation of all or part of an
area proposed for annexation in a previously filed petition that is still
pending approval, denial or rejection.
(Res. R2024-17, passed 8-14-2024)
§ 32.023 CHARACTER OF THE COMMUNITY.
   (A)   The town is located in the west side of the county, near the foothills
of the Oquirrh Mountains. The town shares borders with Eagle Mountain to the
north, and the remaining borders are of unincorporated Utah County.
   (B)   Some of the early residents of the area, the Ute Indians, first used
the valley for their hunting grounds, then, in 1859, Latter Day Saint pioneers
began grazing cattle and sheep in the valley. In 1854 a group of men arrived in
what is now the town, laying out a townsite and building a rock fort. By 1855,
many families, including the Carson, Beardshall and Clegg families had answered
the call to help settle the town. In 1858, Johnston’s Army arrived in the town
and by November 1858, the encampment known as “Camp Floyd” had over 7,000
occupants. After the Civil War broke out, the soldiers were recalled, reducing
the town’s population to less than 50 families. In the early days, the town was
a major stopping point for the Pony Express, the Overland Stage and the Union
Pacific Railroad. The Stagecoach Inn was also used as a telegraph station for a
period of time. Mining and raising sheep were two of the major industries in
the area for many years. The raising of cattle and sheep, along with farming
are still prevalent in the area today but on a smaller scale.
   (C)   The town became an incorporated town in 2004. Today, the town is a
quiet town with a rich history that residents have so far managed to retain and
would like to preserve. Rural living and the historical significance of the
town are key components that the town leaders and residents of the town have
worked hard to maintain as record breaking growth in the area threatens their
way of life. The town residents realize that growth is necessary but they would
like future industry to work with them to preserve the small town atmosphere,
the dark skies, wildlife corridors and the historical sites within the town and
the surrounding area. The town wants to be good neighbors with neighboring
businesses and industry and they feel that this can be accomplished with open
communication and cooperation on both sides.
(Res. R2024-17, passed 8-14-2024)
§ 32.024 MUNICIPAL SERVICES.
   All areas included in the plan will need municipal services. Annexation will
allow residents and developers of annexed property access to culinary water,
sewer systems and electric power services, provided they meet all town
specifications and comply with all applicable development ordinances.
(Res. R2024-17, passed 8-14-2024)
§ 32.025 EXTENSION OF MUNICIPAL SERVICES.
   Where municipal services are not presently extended, services will be
extended on an as-needed basis at the cost of the developer. All extensions of
municipal services must comply with all ordinance and policy criteria, and the
individual developer or property owner will pay for necessary extensions. The
plan and time frame for the extension of municipal services will be determined
by the interest of the property owners to subdivide and develop their ground
and the interest and ability of the town to provide such services. It is in the
interest of town residents to foster orderly sequential development.
(Res. R2024-17, passed 8-14-2024)
§ 32.026 SERVICE FINANCING.
   Municipal services in newly annexed areas will be financed and constructed
by the developer in addition to the town’s collection and investment of impact
fees. Through increases in property valuations and subsequent increases in the
collection of property and sales taxes, inherent increases to the General Fund
will help defray added expenses that the town may incur by annexing new
properties.
(Res. R2024-17, passed 8-14-2024)
§ 32.027 ESTIMATE OF TAX CONSEQUENCES.
   (A)   The annexation area within the town’s area is limited to
unincorporated Utah County properties. Other taxing entities, including, but
not limited to, schools, county, library, sewer, water conservancy and mosquito
abatement, already cover the potential annexation area.
   (B)   The town’s combined property tax rate for tax year 2023 is 0.007501
Utah County’s unincorporated areas’ combined tax rate is 0.0078530, which
includes the same taxing entities listed above, except for the town, but
includes:
      (1)   SA-6 Service Area 6-Law, Zoning;
      (2)   SA-8 Service Area 8-Planning; and
      (3)   SA-9 Service Area 9-Agri-Fire.
   (C)   If annexed into town, residents in an expansion area would recognize a
tax rate decrease of 0.000352. This information is based on the current tax
rate of all applicable taxing entities and recognizes that any of the
respective taxing entities may adjust tax rates as necessary.
(Res. R2024-17, passed 8-14-2024)
§ 32.028 INTERESTS OF AFFECTED ENTITIES.
   (A)   In evaluating a proposed annexation, the interests of all affected
entities should be considered. The annexation does not extend beyond the limits
of the adopted annexation policy plan. Other services needed for the
annexation, e.g., electrical power, internet and communications, are available
or reasonably available for the proposed annexation.
   (B)   The petitioners of annexation have entered into agreement(s) with
affected entities, as applicable, for the provision of required infrastructure
and services.
   (C)   The annexation does not create boundary alignment issues with any
public or charter schools, or affected entities, unless interlocal agreements
have been created to address the alignment issues.
(Res. R2024-17, passed 8-14-2024)
§ 32.029 OTHER CONSIDERATIONS.
   (A)   Attempt to avoid gaps between or overlaps with the expansion areas of
other municipalities. Eagle Mountain shows an expansion area on their south
border in an attempt to surround the town’s borders; but Eagle Mountains
proposed expansion attempts to expand beyond a pinch point in their current
boundaries. Thus, the town’s proposed expansion area simply seeks to extend the
town’s to allow for natural expansion of the town’s borders. Multiple property
owners are within the expansion area.
   (B)   Consider population growth projections for the town and adjoining
areas for the next 20 years. Due to the vacant land in the west corner of Utah
County, population projections are as follows:
 
Entity           2020 Census 2030   2040    2050
Cedar Fort       671         773    1,855   11,845
Eagle Mountain   39,885      65,038 99,064  141,252
Fairfield        152         300    600     900
Saratoga Springs 39,085      79,815 117,641 138,600
 
   (C)   (1)   Consider current and projected costs of infrastructure, urban
services and public facilities necessary to facilitate full development of the
area within the town; and to expand infrastructure, services and facilities
into the area being considered for inclusion in the expansion area.
      (2)   The projected backbone infrastructure costs are estimated to be
millions of dollars to service the area identified in the annexation
declaration map for potential annexation with water, roads and storm drainage
being installed.
   (D)   Consider, in conjunction with the general plan, the need over the next
20 years for additional land suitable for residential, commercial and
industrial development. The town has anticipated annexation petitions to
facilitate desired residential, agricultural and some commercial and industrial
development. Upon receipt of each annexation petition, the town will review
each request for compliance with this subchapter and opportunities to implement
the adopted goals and objectives of the general plan.
   (E)   (1)   Consider the reasons for including agricultural lands, forests,
recreational areas and wildlife management areas in the town.
      (2)   The proposed annexation areas include existing agricultural,
forest, recreational or wildlife management lands. The town anticipates future
annexations of land that preserve open space and facilitate access to
recreational opportunities will benefit residents.
(Res. R2024-17, passed 8-14-2024)
§ 32.030 JUSTIFICATION FOR EXCLUDING LANDS FROM POTENTIAL EXPANSION AREA.
   No developed lands within one-half mile of the town’s existing boundary are
excluded from the potential expansion area, except those lands already
incorporated in other municipalities.
(Res. R2024-17, passed 8-14-2024)
**** TAKINGS POLICY ****
§ 32.045 POLICY CONSIDERATIONS.
   (A)   It is the policy of the town to carefully consider matters involving
claims of constitutional takings. This subchapter serves two purposes:
      (1)   To ensure fairness to property owners asserting such claims; and
      (2)   To acknowledge the legal and financial uncertainty and burden of
defending claims involving takings.
   (B)   The town also affirms its right and duty to regulate land use in a
manner consistent with state and federal law. This includes the authority to
impose lawful dedications and exactions that serve public purposes. The intent
of this subchapter is to establish:
      (1)   A formal procedure for reviewing actions that may involve a taking
of private property; and
      (2)   Clear standards to guide town officials in determining whether
compensation is required or regulation is lawful.
   (C)   An action by the town involving the physical taking or exaction of
private property shall not be considered a constitutional taking under this
subchapter if:
      (1)   The action bears an essential nexus to a legitimate governmental
interest; and
      (2)   The exaction is roughly proportional and reasonably related on an
individualized basis to the nature and extent of the impact caused by the
proposed development on the governmental interest at issue.
(Prior Code, § 1.5.20)
§ 32.046 DEFINITIONS.
   For the purpose of this subchapter, the following definitions shall apply
unless the context clearly indicates or requires a different meaning.
   APPLICANT. A property owner or authorized representative who submits a
request for review of a final decision under this subchapter alleging a
constitutional taking.
   CONSTITUTIONAL TAKING. A governmental action resulting in the physical
taking or regulatory exaction of private real property requiring compensation
under the Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments to the United States Constitution, or
Article I, § 22 of the Utah Constitution.
   ESSENTIAL NEXUS. A clear and direct connection between a legitimate
governmental interest and the exaction or condition imposed by the town.
   EXACTION. A condition or requirement imposed by the town on a land use
application or development approval, which may include the dedication of land,
payment of fees, construction of public improvements or other similar
obligations.
   FINAL DECISION. The last official action taken by any town employee,
officer, board, commission or the Town Council that determines the outcome of a
land use application, enforcement action or development condition, and that
gives rise to a constitutional taking claim.
   LEGITIMATE GOVERNMENTAL INTEREST. An interest that the town is
constitutionally and statutorily empowered to pursue, including, but not
limited to, public health, safety, welfare, land use regulation, environmental
protection and infrastructure development.
   PROPERTY or PRIVATE REAL PROPERTY. Land or interests in land, including any
legally recognized estate, right, title or entitlement held by a private
individual or entity.
   PROPORTIONALITY or ROUGH PROPORTIONALITY. The requirement that an exaction
or condition imposed on a land use application must be roughly equivalent in
nature and extent to the impact of the proposed development, as determined on
an individual property basis, in accordance with established constitutional
standards.
   REVIEWING BODY or REVIEWING OFFICIAL. The Town Council, or any board,
commission, officer or other person designated by the Town Council to conduct a
review pursuant to this subchapter.
(Prior Code, § 1.5.10)
§ 32.047 GUIDELINES ADVISORY.
   (A)   The guidelines adopted and decisions rendered under the provisions of
this subchapter are advisory in nature and shall not be construed to:
      (1)   Expand the town’s liability for a constitutional taking; or
      (2)   Limit the lawful scope of the town’s regulatory authority over real
property.
   (B)   The advisory opinions and reviews conducted under this subchapter do
not create or confer any additional substantive rights or remedies beyond those
otherwise available under applicable state or federal law.
   (C)   No town board, officer or employee shall be required to conduct a
review or render a determination under this subchapter, except as provided in §
32.048.
(Prior Code, § 1.5.30)
§ 32.048 REVIEW OF DECISION.
   (A)   Generally. Any owner of private real property who asserts that a
constitutional taking of their property has occurred may request a review of
the final decision of any town officer, employee, board, commission or the Town
Council. The following procedures govern such review.
      (1)   Final decision requirement. The applicant must first obtain a final
and authoritative determination by the town regarding the action or decision at
issue before requesting review.
      (2)   Filing deadline. Within 30 calendar days from the date of the final
decision, the applicant must file a written request for review with the Town
Recorder/Clerk. A copy of the request shall also be filed with the Town
Attorney.
      (3)   Scheduling of review. The Town Council, or a person or body it
designates, shall immediately schedule a hearing to review the decision that
gave rise to the constitutional takings claim.
   (B)   Required application information. In addition to the written request
for review, the applicant shall submit the following documentation before the
review hearing date:
      (1)   Name of the applicant;
      (2)   Name and business address of the current property owner and form of
ownership (e.g., individual, corporation, partnership);
      (3)   If ownership is through an entity, the names and addresses of all
principal shareholders, partners or members;
      (4)   A detailed explanation of the grounds for claiming a constitutional
taking;
      (5)   A description of the property alleged to have been taken;
      (6)   Evidence of the property’s value, including date and cost of
acquisition, and any change in value before and after the alleged taking;
      (7)   Name of the person or entity from whom the property was acquired,
including any relationship to the applicant;
      (8)   Nature of the claimed protectable interest (e.g., fee simple,
leasehold);
      (9)   Terms, including price, of any sale or purchase of a full or
partial interest in the property within three years prior to the application;
      (10)   All appraisals prepared for financing, sale, taxation or other
purposes in the past three years;
      (11)   Assessed property values and ad valorem tax records for the past
three years;
      (12)   Mortgage or loan details, including lender, interest rate,
balance, term and any transfer provisions;
      (13)   Listings or offers for sale or rent within the last three years,
including price and offer details;
      (14)   All feasibility studies commissioned by the applicant or their
agents within the past three years;
      (15)   For income producing properties, income and expense statements for
the prior three years;
      (16)   Title policy or documentation showing all recorded liens or
encumbrances; and
      (17)   Any additional information requested by the Town Council or its
designee that is reasonably necessary to determine whether a constitutional
taking has occurred.
   (C)   Application completion. An application is not considered complete or
officially submitted until the designated reviewing body certifies receipt of
all required information. The town shall notify the applicant of any missing or
incomplete items.
   (D)   Hearing and evidence. The Town Council, or its designee, shall conduct
the review and consider all evidence submitted by the applicant, the town and
any other interested parties.
   (E)   Decision deadline. A final written decision shall be issued within 14
days from the date the complete application was filed with the Town Recorder/
Clerk. The decision shall be delivered to the applicant and to the town
officer, employee or body whose action is under review.
   (F)   Effect of inaction. If the Town Council or designated reviewer fails
to issue a decision within 14 days of receiving the completed application, the
final decision under review shall be deemed approved by default.
(Prior Code, § 1.5.40)
§ 32.049 REVIEW OF GUIDELINES.
   (A)   The Town Council shall review the facts and supporting documentation
provided by the applicant in order to determine whether the action taken by the
town constitutes a constitutional taking, as defined in this subchapter.
   (B)   In conducting this review, the Town Council shall evaluate the
following criteria:
      (1)   Whether the physical taking or exaction of private real property
bears an essential nexus to a legitimate governmental interest;
      (2)   Whether a legitimate governmental interest exists that justifies
the town’s action; and;
      (3)   Whether the property taken or the exaction imposed is roughly
proportionate and reasonably related, both in nature and extent, on an
individualized property basis, to the impact of the activity or development
that is the subject of the decision under review.
(Prior Code, § 1.5.50)
§ 32.050 RESULTS OF REVIEW.
   (A)   Upon completion of the review described in this subchapter, the
reviewing body or official shall make a formal determination addressing the
constitutional takings issues set forth in this code.
   (B)   If, based on the facts presented and applicable legal standards, the
reviewing body or official determines that a constitutional taking may have
occurred, or that the action in question does not meet the standards
established by this subchapter, the reviewer will:
      (1)   Document the findings and reasoning that support such
determination; and
      (2)   Submit a written recommendation to the Town Council, which may
include any of the following:
         (a)   A recommendation that the Town Council rescind, revise or amend
the decision giving rise to the claim;
         (b)   A recommendation that the Town Council provide compensation or
other remedy consistent with constitutional standards; or
         (c)   A determination that no constitutional taking has occurred, and
that no further action is required.
   (C)   (1)   The Town Council shall consider the recommendation in a timely
manner and take such action as it deems appropriate under the law and in the
public interest.
      (2)   The decision of the Town Council constitutes the town’s final
administrative determination.
(Prior Code, § 1.5.60)
§ 32.051 PROPERTY RIGHTS OMBUDSMAN.
   (A)   In accordance with U.C.A. §§ 13-43-201 et seq., any applicant may
request an advisory opinion from the State Office of the Property Rights
Ombudsman concerning a land use decision or alleged constitutional taking.
   (B)   The town shall cooperate fully with such requests.
(Prior Code, § 1.5.70)
**** SURPLUS PROPERTY POLICY ****
§ 32.065 DEFINITIONS.
   For the purpose of this subchapter, the following definitions shall apply
unless the context clearly indicates or requires a different meaning.
   BONA FIDE CHARITY. A nonprofit entity recognized under I.R.C. § 501(c)(3) or
registered as a nonprofit corporation under state law.
   COMPETITIVE BIDDING. A method of public sale in which the highest
responsible bidder is selected through an open and competitive process.
   COST ACKNOWLEDGMENT. A formal confirmation that a party has received, agreed
to or is responsible for specific costs or fees, such as those associated with
a contract, loan or donation. It serves as official documentation of financial
responsibility to prevent future disputes
   DISPOSAL. The sale, transfer, donation or discarding of town-owned property
in accordance with the procedures established in this section.
   ESTIMATED VALUE. Market value, determined via appraisal, valuation service
or research.
   INTERNAL TRANSFER. Reassignment of surplus property between town
departments.
   PERSONAL PROPERTY. All tangible items owned by the town that are not real
property, including, but not limited to, equipment, furniture, vehicles, tools
and electronic devices.
   PROFESSIONAL PUBLICATION OR VALUATION SERVICE. Industry-standard resources
used to assess the fair market value of surplus property, including trade
journals or valuation platforms.
   PUBLIC NOTICE. Posting notice of the proposed sale or disposal on the town’s
official website and in at least one public location within the town not fewer
than ten days prior to the sale.
   QUALIFIED, INDEPENDENT APPRAISER. Independent, certified professional with
no affiliation with the town.
   REAL PROPERTY. Land and any permanent structures or improvements affixed
thereto, including easements and rights-of-way.
   SALVAGE. Inoperable or beyond repair, and may only be used for parts, scrap
or recycling.
   SIGNIFICANT REAL PROPERTY. Any parcel of real property owned by the town
with an estimated value of $100,000 or more.
   SURPLUS PROPERTY. Any town-owned personal property that is obsolete, unused,
unsuitable, no longer needed or otherwise in excess of the town’s requirements.
(Prior Code, § 1.10.10)
§ 32.066 DISPOSAL OF SURPLUS PERSONAL PROPERTY.
   (A)   For the purpose of this section, the following definitions shall apply
unless the context clearly indicates or requires a different meaning.
      BONA FIDE CHARITY. A nonprofit entity recognized by the Internal Revenue
Service under I.R.C. § 501(c)(3) or a charitable organization recognized by the
state.
      COMPETITIVE BIDDING. A public process for selling surplus property in
which potential buyers submit bids, and the highest responsive and responsible
bid is accepted.
      DESIGNEE. A person or office formally authorized by the Town Council or
Mayor to act on their behalf.
      DISPOSAL. The sale, transfer, donation or discarding of town-owned
property in accordance with the procedures established in this section.
      ESTIMATED VALUE. The market value of surplus property as reasonably
determined by the Mayor or designee using methods including, but not limited
to, appraisal, market research or valuation services.
      HIGHEST AND BEST ECONOMIC RETURN. The method of sale or transfer that
reasonably maximizes the financial or practical benefit to the town, determined
by methods such as competitive bidding, appraisal, market survey or auction.
      INTERNAL TRANSFER. The reassignment of surplus property from one town
department to another for continued municipal use, as authorized by the Mayor
or designee.
      INVENTORY CONTROL. The official record maintained by the town documenting
the ownership, status and disposition of town property.
      PERSONAL PROPERTY. All tangible items owned by the town that are not real
property, including, but not limited to, equipment, furniture, vehicles, tools
and electronic devices.
      PROFESSIONAL PUBLICATION OR VALUATION SERVICE. An industry-standard
resource used to assess the fair market value of surplus property, including
trade journals or valuation platforms.
      PUBLIC NOTICE. Posting notice of the proposed sale or disposal on the
town’s official website and in at least one public location within the town not
fewer than ten days prior to the sale.
      QUALIFIED, INDEPENDENT APPRAISER. A certified or professionally
recognized individual who is not affiliated with the town and is competent to
determine the value of the property.
      REAL PROPERTY. Land and any permanent structures or improvements affixed
thereto, including easements and rights-of-way.
      SALVAGE. Property that is inoperable or beyond repair and may only be
used for parts, scrap or recycling.
      SALVAGE OR JUNK YARD. A licensed facility that receives discarded or
damaged goods for recycling, parts or disposal.
      SIGNIFICANT REAL PROPERTY. Any parcel of real property owned by the town
with an estimated value of $100,000 or more.
      SURPLUS PROPERTY. Any town-owned personal property that is obsolete,
unused, unsuitable, no longer needed or otherwise in excess of the town’s
requirements.
   (B)   Town-owned personal property, excluding consumables used in daily
operations, shall only be disposed of in accordance with this subchapter.
   (C)   When a department identifies personal property as surplus, obsolete,
unused or no longer needed:
      (1)   The department head shall notify the Mayor;
      (2)   The Mayor shall notify other departments to determine internal
interest;
      (3)   If another department has need of the property, the Mayor shall
arrange an internal transfer and update inventory records; or
      (4)   If no department has need of the property, the Mayor shall proceed
with disposal;
   (D)   For property valued at $2,000 or more:
      (1)   The Mayor shall prepare a list of such property and submit it to
the Town Council for approval by resolution;
      (2)   Upon approval, the Mayor shall sell the property to achieve the
highest and best economic return using one or more of the following:
         (a)   Competitive bidding;
         (b)   Independent appraisal;
         (c)   Professional valuation services; or
         (d)   Informal market survey.
      (3)   Public notice of the sale shall be posted in three public locations
at least ten days prior to the sale; and
      (4)   Proceeds shall be credited to the town’s General Fund;
   (E)   For property valued under $2,000:
      (1)   The Mayor may dispose of such property without consent of the Town
Council; and
      (2)   Disposal may include donation to a bona fide charity, salvage or
landfill use.
(Prior Code, § 1.10.20)
§ 32.067 DISPOSAL OF TOWN-OWNED LAND.
   (A)   Land owned by the town shall be classified as either:
      (1)   INSIGNIFICANT LAND. Land that may be considered eligible for
disposal without Town Council approval; or
      (2)   SIGNIFICANT LAND. Land not eligible for disposal without Town
Council approval.
   (B)   Significant land includes:
      (1)   Historically significant land (e.g., Pony Express Trail, viewsheds,
scenic corridors);
      (2)   Ecologically sensitive land (e.g., steep slopes, wildlife habitat,
drainage corridors);
      (3)   Operational sites (e.g., Town Hall, fire stations, utility
facilities); and
      (4)   Recreational land (e.g., parks, trails, natural open space).
   (C)   Insignificant land includes:
      (1)   Unused easements or rights-of-way;
      (2)   Isolated, remnant or unimproved parcels not intended as buffer or
open space;
      (3)   Land with no future anticipated use or public purpose;
      (4)   Land not classified as historically or ecologically significant;
      (5)   Parcels whose disposal does not violate development code;
      (6)   Land that no longer serves its intended purpose; and
      (7)   Entire contiguous parcels not mapped as significant.
(Prior Code, § 1.10.30)
§ 32.068 LAND DISPOSAL APPLICATION.
   (A)   Applications to dispose of land shall be submitted to the Town
Recorder/Clerk and include:
      (1)   Applicant’s name and address;
      (2)   Map, sketch or legal description of the parcel;
      (3)   Classification as significant or insignificant land;
      (4)   Survey and plat (required for insignificant land); and
      (5)   Proof that the applicant owns adjacent land.
   (B)   The application process is as follows.
      (1)   The Recorder/Clerk shall evaluate the classification.
      (2)   The Recorder/Clerk shall notify all adjacent landowners.
      (3)   For insignificant land, objections must be submitted within ten
days.
      (4)   The Recorder/Clerk shall provide a recommendation to the Mayor, who
will then approve, modify or deny the application.
      (5)   Valuation shall be based on the average value of unimproved
agricultural land within five miles.
      (6)   Applicants and objectors shall have the opportunity to present
their positions to the Mayor.
(Prior Code, § 1.10.40)
§ 32.069 DECISION ON APPLICATION.
   (A)   The Mayor shall make a final decision on the application and notify
all parties.
   (B)   The Town Recorder/Clerk shall process approved applications.
   (C)   Appeals may be submitted within 30 days to the Town Council.
   (D)   The Town Council may:
      (1)   Affirm the decision;
      (2)   Reverse the decision; or
      (3)   Request reconsideration by the Mayor with specific findings.
   (E)   One additional appeal may be submitted. The second decision shall be
final.
(Prior Code, § 1.10.50)
§ 32.070 PAYMENT.
   (A)   Payment shall be required for all property disposals.
   (B)   Fair market value shall be based upon fair market value as determined
by an independent appraisal or other appropriate valuation method approved by
the Town Council.
(Prior Code, § 1.10.60)
§ 32.071 DISPOSAL OF SIGNIFICANT LAND.
   (A)   Applications for disposal of significant land shall:
      (1)   Include a legal description or parcel number; and
      (2)   Optionally include proposed uses, access conditions or value
estimate.
   (B)   The application shall be:
      (1)   Reviewed by all town departments and the Mayor;
      (2)   Subject to a public hearing by the Town Council; and
      (3)   Noticed by mail to adjacent landowners and published publicly 14
days before the hearing.
   (C)   The applicant shall pay all processing and notice costs.
   (D)   The Town Council may:
      (1)   Impose conditions such as a minimum sale price or specific use; and
      (2)   Select the disposal method (e.g., realtor, auction, direct sale).
(Prior Code, § 1.10.70)
§ 32.072 COST ACKNOWLEDGMENT.
   (A)   Purchasers must sign a cost acknowledgment form affirming
responsibility for all disposal process costs.
   (B)   Costs are itemized in Exhibit 1 of the ordinance codified in this
section and are on file in the Recorder/Clerk’s office.
(Prior Code, § 1.10.80)
§ 32.073 TRADE IN AUTHORITY.
   The Mayor may authorize the trade in of surplus equipment as part of a
procurement transaction if it is determined to be in the best interest of the
town.
(Prior Code, § 1.10.90)
§ 32.074 RECORDKEEPING AND ANNUAL REPORT.
   (A)   The Town Recorder/Clerk shall maintain records of all surplus property
transactions.
   (B)   The Mayor shall provide an annual report to the Town Council
summarizing items disposed of, method of disposal and proceeds.
(Prior Code, § 1.10.100)
**** PURCHASING POLICY ****
§ 32.085 PURPOSE.
   (A)   All procurement on behalf of the town shall be conducted in accordance
with rules and regulations adopted by the Town Council, as amended from time to
time.
   (B)   (1)   This subchapter establishes operational policies for the town’s
purchasing process, which assure the community that goods and services required
to support the operation of town government are procured in a manner consistent
with provisions of the town’s code, state code, administrative rules and
federal laws, where applicable.
      (2)   (a)   The town is committed to fairness and equal opportunity with
integrity and openness that results in the best value for the town. The
statements contained in this subchapter represent the basic intentions and
goals of the town.
         (b)   Nothing in this statement shall create rights or interests in
third parties, impose obligations upon or create causes of action against the
town, its officers, agents or employees. Failure to follow the procedures set
forth herein may be remedied by a Town Council determination, as defined in
this subchapter, unless otherwise provided by law.
(Ord. 2024-11, passed 10-16-2024)
§ 32.086 DEFINITIONS.
   For the purpose of this subchapter, the following definitions shall apply
unless the context clearly indicates or requires a different meaning.
   ADDENDUM or AMENDMENT. Any written modification or revision to any bid
document or contract document.
   BID. Unless otherwise specified, represents all forms of solicitation,
including, but not limited to, request for quote (RFQ), invitation for bid
(IFB), request for proposal (RFP) and request for statement of qualifications
(RFSQ).
   COMPETITIVE SEALED BIDDING. A process in which vendors are invited to submit
formal sealed bids to provide a designated product or to complete a designated
project in accordance with specifications provided by the town.
   COMMODITY. Goods or services.
   CONTRACT. All types of town agreements, regardless of what they may be
called, for the purchase or disposal of real or personal property, goods or
services.
   COOPERATIVE PROCUREMENTS. The combining of requirements for two or more
purchasing units outside the town, in order to obtain the benefits of volume
purchases and/or reduction in administrative efforts and costs.
   EMERGENCY PURCHASE. A purchase that must be made quickly that would not be
practical to go through the procurement process. Failure to anticipate a need
or situation created by improper planning or negligence is not to be considered
an emergency.
   DECLARED EMERGENCY. Emergency or disaster situation where the need for
response exceeds all capabilities. A condition that requires emergency
assistance to save lives and/or to protect property, public health and safety,
and to reduce the threat and effects of a disaster. A DECLARATION OF EMERGENCY
is necessary to access specified extraordinary powers considered necessary to
prevent, respond to or alleviate the effects of the emergency or disaster.
   DESIGNATED COUNCIL MEMBER. The person designated by the Town Council to
ensure compliance with the purchasing policy.
   GOOD. A tangible product that is not money or real estate. The term GOOD
shall be interchangeable with the terms SUPPLY, MERCHANDISE, PRODUCT, MATERIAL,
ITEM, PERSONAL PROPERTY and the like, for the purpose of this subchapter.
   IMMATERIAL ERROR. An irregularity or abnormality that is a matter of form
that does not affect substance, or an inconsequential variation from a
requirement of a solicitation that has no, little or trivial effect on the
procurement process and that is not prejudicial to other vendors.
   INFORMAL QUOTE. A process in which requests for a quote are sent directly to
vendors to obtain pricing from any authorized buyer for the town.
   INSUFFICIENT RESPONSE.
      (1)   Where one less response is received to any invitation for bid
(IFB), request for proposal (RFP) or request for statement of qualifications
(RFSQ); or
      (2)   Where two or fewer quotes are received in response to an RFQ.
   INTENT TO NEGOTIATE. Component of a competitive bidding process involving
negotiating terms and conditions with multiple potential vendors before
contract award.
   INVITATION FOR BID (IFB). A solicitation process where bids are solicited
from potential vendors. The term INVITATION FOR BID shall be interchangeable
with the term REQUEST FOR BID for the purpose of this subchapter. IFBs shall be
generally used for construction projects.
   NONCOMPETITIVE PURCHASE. The purchase of a good or service directly from a
supplier without a competitive process.
   PROFESSIONAL SERVICES. Labor, effort or work that requires an elevated
degree of specialized knowledge and discretion, including, but not limited to,
labor, effort or work in the field of:
      (1)   Accounting;
      (2)   Architecture;
      (3)   Artistic endeavors;
      (4)   Construction design and management;
      (5)   Engineering;
      (6)   Financial services;
      (7)   Information technology;
      (8)   Insurance;
      (9)   Law;
      (10)   Lobbying;
      (11)   Medicine;
      (12)   Mental health services;
      (13)   General plan planning; and
      (14)   Underwriting software.
   PROJECT MANAGER (PM). The person designated by the town, who is in charge of
managing a specific purchase or project.
   PROTESTOR. One who has standing to file a protest to challenge the award or
proposed award of a contract for the procurement of goods and services.
   PURCHASING. The process of buying, procuring, renting, leasing or otherwise
acquiring any commodity. The term PURCHASING shall be interchangeable with the
term PROCUREMENT for the purpose of this subchapter. It also includes all
functions that pertain to the obtaining of any commodity, including:
      (1)   Description of requirements;
      (2)   Selection and solicitation of bids, proposals, qualifications or
quotes;
      (3)   Preparation and award of contract; and
      (4)   All phases of contract administration
   PURCHASING OFFICER. The Town Administrator or designee. The PURCHASING
OFFICER shall oversee the town’s purchasing functions and ensure purchases
align with this subchapter.
   PURCHASING TOOLS. The town’s preferred methods of advertising and hosting
solicitations.
   RELATED PARTY. Any party, whether an individual, corporation, partnership,
association, limited liability company or any other form of business
association or entity whatsoever related to any vendor by blood, marriage,
ownership or contract within the first degree of consanguinity, through which
the party has a relationship of ownership, or other interest with the vendor,
so that the party will actually, or by effect, receive or control a portion of
the benefit or profit.
   REQUEST FOR INFORMATION (RFI). A solicitation process where written
information, comments or suggestions are requested from potential vendors. An
RFI is not a bid process resulting in a purchase or contract.
   REQUEST FOR PROPOSAL (RFP). A solicitation process where proposals are
solicited from potential vendors.
   REQUEST FOR QUOTE (RFQ). A solicitation process where signed quotes are
obtained from potential vendors. RFQs shall generally be used when purchasing
goods.
   REQUEST FOR STATEMENT OF QUALIFICATIONS (RFSQ). A solicitation process where
qualifications are solicited from potential vendors.
